items.title: US authorities seize domains behind a China-based firm’s scanning tool whose targets included airports in Japan and Poland
items.content_text: On 8 October the Justice Department and FBI announced court-authorised seizures, in the Western District of Pennsylvania, of domains behind two tools: Microscan, a Python web application with more than 1,300 penetration-testing scripts supported by a Mirai-variant IoT botnet, and FishHub, a spear-phishing and malware-delivery platform. US authorities say China-based Integrity Technology Group built and ran them; CyberScoop calls the tools Flax Typhoon-linked, while Cybersecurity Dive says the activity mimics that group. Court documents list Microscan targets including airports in Japan and Poland, a South Carolina power company and gas and power firms in Taiwan; FishHub went after Taiwanese universities. Neither report confirms that any airport was breached. A joint FBI, CISA and NSA advisory, AA26-281A, describes scanning, cross-site scripting, Exchange password spraying and persistence through VPN software. It leads this page because it is the only item in the window that names aviation infrastructure.

items.title: Attackers took over refrigeration controllers at about 700 French supermarkets — a warning for every internet-reachable building controller on an airport estate
items.content_text: Over the nights of 11–13 October, attackers remotely changed settings on web-managed refrigeration controllers in French supermarkets, forcing long defrost cycles with temperatures reported as high as about 50°C, spoiling stock and, according to the Paris prosecutor, starting fires at some stores. Finance Minister Roland Lescure told Parliament on 13 October that about 700 of France’s roughly 10,000 supermarkets were affected, and Carrefour, Coopérative U, E.Leclerc, Intermarché and Monoprix have confirmed impact. CERT-FR’s alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012 named Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers on 12 October, added Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb on 13 October, and in its 16 October update says the campaigns are probably still running. Danfoss and Copeland both say most affected units are older or end-of-life models. No group has claimed the attack, no ransom has been demanded and the entry route has not been established; the prosecutor’s cybercrime section has assigned the inquiry to OFAC, France’s anti-cybercrime office. This is not an aviation incident and it does not count toward this page’s threat level. Our assessment of why it is here: airport terminals, flight-catering units and cargo cold stores run the same class of remotely managed refrigeration and building controllers, often maintained by a contractor through a web interface, and this attack shows how directly a changed setpoint becomes physical loss.

items.title: Berlin Brandenburg stops all flying for 45 minutes on a drone sighting, its 28th drone this year against eight in all of 2025 — the gap is detection, not defence
items.content_text: On the evening of Wednesday 23 September, Germany’s air navigation service DFS closed Berlin Brandenburg’s northern runway after a drone was sighted at about 20:00 local time. It closed the southern runway at 20:20 and lifted the closure at 21:05, dpa reports, leaving the airport with no take-offs or landings for about 45 minutes. Numerous flights were delayed and several were diverted. The Federal Police searched and found nothing, and Brandenburg police have opened an investigation into dangerous interference with air traffic. No operator or motive has been identified. Some early English-language reports gave the closure as about five minutes, apparently misreading the time zone; dpa’s timeline gives 45. The trend matters more than the single event. DFS figures reported by dpa put drones recorded at BER at 28 in the first half of 2026, against eight in the whole of 2025, and flying was suspended seven times in the half-year. Earlier in the month, Brussels Airport halted traffic for roughly half an hour on the evening of Friday 12 September after a drone was sighted near the airfield; no injuries or damage were reported and movements resumed once the area was cleared, with the drone’s origin and intent unattributed. The following day Vilnius closed for 38 minutes on a drone alert that scrambled a NATO jet before the object was confirmed to be a flock of birds. Both follow the US Labor Day weekend incursion at San Diego that grounded around 400 flights, where the TSA reportedly could not identify the operator and coverage noted that US airports carry no mandatory drone-detection requirement at all. None of this is a cyberattack and none of it should be filed as one. It belongs on this page because the operational consequence is identical to an OT failure and lands on the same people: a ground stop cascades into stand and gate reallocation, jet-bridge and ramp re-sequencing, baggage re-flow and fuel and de-icing re-planning, and the decision to stop or resume is increasingly taken from software — counter-UAS detection feeds, ground-movement displays, airfield lighting control — that few airports treat as operational technology with an integrity requirement. Vilnius is the instructive one: the cost was not the drone, it was the ambiguity.

items.title: UK air traffic failure traced to a software defect in aircraft code allocation — NATS’ preliminary report describes a timing fault, not an attack
items.content_text: This is not a cyber incident. It is carried here, clearly labelled, because it is the aviation infrastructure story of the period and readers will reasonably have wondered. On 8 September a failure at NATS, the UK air navigation service provider, forced Heathrow to suspend arrivals and disrupted Gatwick and Manchester, affecting more than 2,000 flights across 8–9 September. NATS’ preliminary report, published on 18 September, places the cause in a small part of the National Airspace System: a software defect in the code that allocates aircraft identification codes. A code request was paused when a higher-priority task pre-empted it, and the update did not complete; Reuters quotes the report as saying that had the higher-priority request arrived “even one millisecond earlier or later, the update would have completed normally.” Restrictions lasted about six hours and clearing the backlog took more than two days. NATS says a mitigation is in place while a permanent fix is safety-tested and deployed. Chief executive Martin Rolfe, who had already ruled out cyber on 10 September, dismissed speculation of military interference and said the fault is unrelated to the 2023 outage; the early accounts blaming an anomalous military flight plan are not supported by the stated cause. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander called the failure “completely unacceptable” and has tasked the Civil Aviation Authority with an independent review of NATS’ findings, its resilience investment plans and regulatory accountability. A full report is to follow, and NATS proposes a further £1bn of investment by 2033. For aviation OT teams the lesson is availability engineering rather than attack defence: a defect that only surfaces when two tasks collide within a millisecond is exactly the kind of fault conventional testing can miss, so the useful questions are how your own flight-critical systems behave when an update stalls and how quickly you recover when one does. Addendum, 21 September: FlightGlobal reports that a separate “connectivity” issue at NATS’ Prestwick centre in Scotland caused delays at several airports less than two weeks after the 8 September failure. No cause has been published, NATS has not linked it to the earlier defect, and nothing in the reporting suggests a cyber element. We carry it as an unattributed operational fault and will update if NATS publishes a cause.

items.title: FBI and Secret Service: the FortiBleed credential campaign against FortiGate VPNs is still running, and their advisory covers every critical-infrastructure sector, transportation included
items.content_text: On Tuesday 6 October the FBI and the US Secret Service issued joint advisory JCSA-20261006-01 warning that the FortiBleed campaign remains active: attackers are still scanning internet-facing Fortinet firewalls and SSL VPN gateways and logging in with credentials obtained earlier. There is no CVE. The agencies tie the campaign to reused or leaked passwords and legacy SHA-256 password storage; researchers describe password spraying and stuffing from leak dumps, offline cracking of extracted hashes and a sniffer that captures authentication traffic across 24 protocols. Some owners were locked out after the intruders created their own administrator accounts and deleted or reset the real ones. The access is resold, the FBI links it to Payload ransomware, and SOCRadar says it has confirmed at least 12 ransomware deployments from it. SOCRadar’s figure of more than 86,644 working device credentials in 194 countries dates from 19 June; it is not a new count. The advisory says it applies to all 16 US critical-infrastructure sectors and names transportation systems among them, and Cybersecurity Dive reports that targeted organisations span every one of the 16. No OT system compromise has been described and no aviation victim is named. Our assessment: FortiGate is a common boundary device between airport and airline corporate networks and terminal and airfield systems, so a stolen admin login there is a stolen boundary.

items.title: GAO: the FAA cannot see spectrum attacks on aircraft communications in real time, and the ACARS and CPDLC datalinks could carry a forged clearance
items.content_text: The US Government Accountability Office published GAO-26-108439 on 21 September, titled “Aviation Cybersecurity: Enhanced Air Safety Requires FAA to Better Mitigate Threats to Aircraft Communications.” Auditors examined the text-based datalinks that carry messages between aircraft, airline operations and air traffic control — ACARS and Controller-Pilot Data Link Communications — and found weaknesses in authentication, encryption and protocol design such that, in GAO’s words, “a malicious actor could transmit fraudulent clearance cancellations, possibly leading to flight delays or safety issues.” On the spectrum side, GAO found that the FAA acknowledges jamming and spoofing as threats but “did not have a defined, real-time monitoring and detection capability for all spectrum-related threats,” and that its risk assessments and security documentation for the National Airspace System are incomplete. GAO makes nine recommendations, covering NAS risk assessments, real-time spectrum-threat monitoring, interagency coordination and stronger authentication and encryption for aircraft communications; the Department of Transportation concurred with all nine, and all nine were open at publication. This is an audit, not an incident. GAO reports no exploitation of either weakness; the report is carried because it is the most substantive primary-source aviation item of the fortnight, not because anything happened. It matters to this page for two reasons. The datalink finding belongs to airlines and their communications providers, and it puts on the record that a message channel crews act on is not authenticated. The spectrum finding is the same problem the Jammertest work exposed for GNSS, stated at national scale: a signal that is manipulated rather than removed produces no alarm anywhere in the chain, and nobody currently owns detecting it.

items.title: Galileo’s encrypted test signal kept a receiver on the right position under spoofing at Jammertest, while a commercial receiver was led astray
items.content_text: On the afternoon of 16 September, five operational Galileo satellites broadcast a new encrypted test signal over Europe for two hours, and receivers at Andøya in Norway and at ESA’s ESTEC navigation laboratory in the Netherlands fixed their positions from it, ESA reported. The signal belongs to Galileo’s Signal Authentication Service (SAS), which uses encrypted ranging signals and is designed to work with OSNMA, the navigation-message authentication service operating since 2025, so that receivers can detect and reject a wide range of spoofing. In a spoofing run at Jammertest, the annual September interference exercise in Norway, the SAS-enabled receiver held its true position while a commercial receiver fed the same false signal calculated wrong ones. EUSPA, the European Commission, ESA and industry plan validation and accreditation in 2027, after which the service is to be declared operational; both SAS and OSNMA are to be free and available worldwide. The same exercise showed why it matters: TechSpot reported on 10 September that researchers spoofed a rescue helicopter’s GPS until its display showed a false track over the Norwegian Sea while the aircraft flew normally. Jamming shows up as signal loss and crews are trained for it; spoofing leaves a receiver confidently reporting a plausible, wrong answer. For airports the exposure runs beyond the flight deck to GNSS-disciplined clocks behind surveillance, surface-movement and logging systems. Authentication belongs on the receiver roadmap; it is not yet today’s mitigation.

items.title: Recorded Future judges Russia’s hybrid activity in Europe opportunistic but likely to escalate — and an alleged sabotage plot against Leipzig/Halle Airport cargo infrastructure is on its list
items.content_text: Recorded Future’s Insikt Group published “Russia Escalating Hybrid Attacks across Europe” on 24 September. It assesses that Russia has escalated what Insikt calls New Generation Warfare tactics in Europe since February 2022, describes current activity as “largely opportunistic”, and judges that Russia is likely to escalate over the next two years, potentially culminating in a full-scale campaign. The incidents it cites include an alleged sabotage plot involving explosives against cargo infrastructure at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August 2026, Russian drones in Estonian airspace on 1 September, an explosive maritime drone intercepted near Romania’s Neptun Deep offshore gas field on 20 August, and DDoS and access operations against the Norwegian public sector; Dark Reading’s coverage on 25 September adds water and wastewater targeting in Norway and Poland. This is an analytic assessment, not a report of a new incident, and the attribution to Russia is at assessment level, with no specific unit named. Insikt’s analyst says that “outside of traditional critical infrastructure, logistics and dual-use firms are at high risk.” For aviation the relevance is the mix. A cargo-hub sabotage plot and drone incursions are physical, not cyber, but they land on the same operations centres, perimeter systems and contractor populations that a cyber intrusion would. Insikt’s recommendations — contractor and insider vetting, perimeter detection and anti-drone measures, law-enforcement partnerships, alternative supply routes, coordination with national CERTs and phishing-resistant MFA — read as a checklist for airports and air-cargo operators.

items.title: Two trackers, two August records: NCC Group counts 1,073 ransomware attacks and Comparitech 997 — and a newer group, Aurora, lists transportation among its targets
items.content_text: NCC Group’s review of August 2026, reported by Industrial Cyber on 28 September, counted 1,073 ransomware attacks, up 12% on July’s 960, which Industrial Cyber reports as a 2026 high. The industrial sector accounted for 329 attacks, about 31%; North America for 473, about 44%; and Europe for 276, about 26%. Qilin led with 164 attacks, about 15%, overtaking The Gentlemen, and DragonForce was also active. NCC also profiles Aurora, a ransomware-as-a-service group active since late April 2026 that targets manufacturing, legal, research and development and transportation organisations through weak or unauthenticated VPN access and PowerShell credential harvesting, then encrypts hypervisors. Comparitech, reported on 14 September, counted 997 attacks in August, a 23% rise on July’s 809 and above its previous monthly record of 988, with utility, healthcare and business-services attacks behind the rise. The two figures differ because the trackers count differently; both rest on leak-site claims and disclosures, a claimed victim is not a confirmed one, and neither describes confirmed OT downtime. For aviation the useful detail is Aurora’s way in. Weak VPN authentication is exactly the gap that integrator and contractor remote access into airports tends to leave, and encrypting the hypervisor takes down every virtual server on it at once — which is how a back-office ransomware event becomes a check-in, baggage or turnaround outage.

items.title: Nozomi’s summer telemetry puts transportation second for OT and IoT alerts per customer, behind only manufacturing
items.content_text: Nozomi Networks Labs’ report on June to August 2026, published 12 October, ranks manufacturing first by alerts per organisation, transportation second, and energy, utilities and waste third, displacing government. About a third of detections involved credential-related techniques. Among alerts Nozomi attributes to a named actor, Scattered Spider accounted for close to half, and Russia-linked or Russian-speaking actors together for more than a third. Siemens PLCs and Rockwell products were among the vulnerable products detected most often, and Nozomi says 58% of the vulnerabilities published in 2026 rate High or Critical, against 48% in 2025. Read the numbers for what they are: alerts per customer across Nozomi’s own installed base, which measures detection activity, not confirmed attacks, and the report does not break transportation down by mode. For airports and airlines the useful signal is the weighting toward credentials, because accounts and logins are where integrator, handler and vendor access lives.

items.title: Forescout studied 47,700 network segments and found only 13% of those holding OT devices were OT-only — the segmentation question airports tend to assume is already answered
items.content_text: Forescout’s Vedere Labs research, published on 22 September and reported by Industrial Cyber on 24 September, analysed 47,700 network segments containing more than 2.5 million devices across 209 organisations. Of the segments that contained OT devices, only 13% were OT-only; the rest also held other types of device, and almost half mixed OT with both IT and IoT assets. Forescout measures the average number of devices per segment as a “blast radius”: 29 in manufacturing and in government, 9 in utilities, 72 in oil and gas and 116 in healthcare. Aviation and transport are not among the sectors it breaks out, and the study describes no incident. Our assessment of the read-across: a terminal network carries BMS, baggage-handling, access-control, CCTV and passenger-facing IoT alongside corporate IT, much of it installed by different integrators at different times, so the finding that OT rarely sits in a segment of its own is a reasonable default assumption until your own inventory proves otherwise.

items.title: Dragos says old worms such as Conficker and WannaCry keep turning up in OT networks — and that a careless cleanup can do more harm than the infection
items.content_text: In a post published 15 October, Dragos’s Lesley Carhart and Jan Hoff say requests for help with legacy commodity infections — Sality, Gammima, WannaCry and Conficker among them — have risen sharply in recent years. Many OT networks Dragos is called into carry 20 to 70 distinct commodity-malware variants spread across several subnets, often on machines older than Windows XP SP2. They attribute the rise to more networking and remote access, better visibility, and rules that require critical-infrastructure networks to be clean, and they set out a “Now / Next / Never” framework, with a white paper, for deciding what to remove and when. Their main warning is that a badly planned removal can cause more operational damage than the malware itself. Nothing here is a targeted campaign. Our assessment for this page: workstations that run baggage handling, airfield lighting and building management at airports often sit on old Windows builds that cannot be patched or rebooted on demand, so the same triage question applies before anyone runs a cleanup tool.

items.title: A three-flaw chain gives attackers root on fully patched Ivanti Connect Secure VPNs — one CVE is fixed and in KEV, the privilege-escalation link is not
items.content_text: Ivanti disclosed CVE-2026-104935 on 13 October: an authentication bypass in Connect Secure that, together with a file-write flaw, lets a remote unauthenticated attacker run commands (CVSS v3.1 8.6, Ivanti). Both flaws are fixed under that single CVE in 22.8R2.5, 25.1.1.2 and 25.1.3.0/25.1.3.1. A third bug, a privilege escalation in the dsinvoked broker, completes the chain to root; it has no CVE and no patch yet, with a fix promised over the coming weeks. Volexity found the chain while responding to an intrusion and attributes it to a new actor it tracks as UTA0576. Exploitation began in early October — Volexity’s case dates from 3 October and Defused saw activity from 1 October — against an appliance that was fully patched at the time. The intruders left no web shell, ran commands through the exploit requests themselves, stole LDAP and domain credentials, queried Active Directory for LAPS passwords and BitLocker keys, Kerberoasted, sprayed passwords and wiped Ivanti debug and Linux audit logs. CISA added the CVE to KEV on 13 October with a 16 October deadline. CISA and Volexity warn that Ivanti’s Integrity Checker Tool may not detect a compromise; Volexity says the chain patches library code in memory and restores configuration data, so a clean result is not proof. Ivanti says a limited number of customers were affected, and no aviation victim is named. Our assessment: Connect Secure is a common route into airline operations and engineering systems and for integrator access to terminal estates, and directory credentials taken through the VPN outlive the patch.

items.title: Citrix NetScaler: three zero-days exploited since late summer, and a fourth critical SAML flaw means some appliances patched last month need upgrading again
items.content_text: Citrix’s NetScaler ADC and Gateway have had three exploited zero-days in little more than a week. CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 (each CVSS v4 9.5) were patched on 27 September in bulletin CTX697096 and added to KEV that day; CVE-2026-88779, which Citrix and watchTowr describe as a denial-of-service flaw affecting appliances configured as a SAML provider (CVSS v4 8.7, bulletin CTX697174), followed into KEV on 4 October. CISA has since warned that attackers use CVE-2026-88779 to force reboots so that code planted through CVE-2026-88771 runs. Google’s threat intelligence group traces the activity to at least 3 September and Palo Alto Networks to 21 August; Mandiant counts dozens of affected organisations across North America and Europe and describes actors with suspected state-nexus links, naming no group. Arctic Wolf’s figure of 78 counts targeted organisations, not confirmed compromises. On 8 October Citrix published CTX697191 for a fourth flaw, CVE-2026-107406 (CVSS v4 9.5), a memory overflow on appliances configured as a SAML service provider or identity provider that Citrix says may lead to code execution or denial of service. It is not reported exploited and was not in KEV as of the 15 October catalog. The builds that fixed the September zero-days stay vulnerable to it when the appliance is a SAML identity provider, so those appliances must be upgraded again; fixed builds are 14.1-73.46 (including FIPS), 13.1-64.29 and, for FIPS/NDcPP, 13.1-37.283, or later. Shadowserver counts more than 20,000 exposed or potentially vulnerable appliances. No airport, airline or air navigation service provider has been named. Our assessment: NetScaler Gateway fronts crew and operations portals, MRO applications and integrator access into terminal systems, and as Mandiant has stressed, upgrading does not remove an intruder who is already in or recover stolen credentials.

items.title: Check Point firewalls are being exploited through the VPN handshake, and a separate management-server flaw was in use two months before a fix — both entered KEV on 22 September
items.content_text: Check Point published a security advisory on 22 September confirming active exploitation of two separate critical flaws. The sources checked for this edition give no CVSS score for either, so none is printed here. The first, CVE-2026-85102, is in Security Gateways and Spark firewalls: improper validation of certificate data during VPN negotiation lets an unauthenticated attacker execute code on the gateway. Check Point released the fix on 9 September and writes that “starting September 12, 2026, we observed a wave of exploitation attempts against Spark customers”; it gives no customer count and no attribution, and publishes indicators in the form of exploitation certificates with the subjects CN=vpn, CN=vpn-user or CN=vpnuser, OU=users, O=global. The second, CVE-2026-93616, is a pre-authentication path traversal in the Security Management web service that leads to script execution or Java class loading. Check Point says it was used in “a handful of pinpointed attacks on July 23, 2026”, about two months before the fix became available on 22 September. It is not CVE-2026-91843, the earlier management-server username flaw, which is still not reported as exploited. CISA added both flaws to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 22 September with a federal deadline of 25 September, in the same batch as Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator and F5 BIG-IP APM. That deadline passed on 25 September. This edition’s research found no further KEV action on either flaw, and no attribution or victim count, as of 6 October. No airport, airline or air navigation service provider has been named as a victim. Our assessment of where it sits in aviation: Spark is Check Point’s small-office firewall line, the class of appliance fitted at outlying sites such as NAVAID and radar shelters, fuel farms, cargo sheds and contractor offices, and often run by a managed-service provider. Check Point gateways also terminate the remote-access VPNs that integrators use to reach terminal BMS, baggage and airfield-lighting systems. The management server is the bigger prize, because it holds the policy for every gateway it manages.

items.title: Fortinet’s FortiMail has an exploited CVSS 9.8 flaw that lets an unauthenticated attacker write files to the appliance — in KEV since 1 October, with fixed releases listed in Fortinet’s 5 October update
items.content_text: Fortinet published PSIRT advisory FG-IR-26-175 on 1 October for CVE-2026-104286 in its FortiMail email security gateway: a path traversal combined with improper handling of NULL bytes that lets an unauthenticated attacker write arbitrary files on the underlying system with crafted HTTP or HTTPS requests. Fortinet scores it CVSS v3 9.8, says it has been reported as exploited in the wild, and found it internally. Affected releases are 7.2.0 to 7.2.9, 7.4.0 to 7.4.8, 7.6.0 to 7.6.6 and 8.0.0 to 8.0.1. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 1 October with a three-day federal deadline of 4 October, which has passed. When the advisory first appeared, fixed releases were planned but undated; Fortinet’s 5 October update lists fixed releases 7.4.9, 7.6.7 and 8.0.2, and tells 7.2 customers to move to the 7.4 branch or later. Fortinet’s workarounds are to disable Identity-Based Encryption (IBE), restrict webmail and management access to trusted networks, and use web-application-firewall rules that block POST requests containing ../ to /ibe paths. No actor, victim or targeted sector has been disclosed. This is not an OT product, and no airport or airline is named. Our assessment of why it is carried: a mail gateway is internet-facing by design, so at an airport authority, airline, ground handler or MRO an unauthenticated file-write flaw on it is a foothold on the corporate edge, and the corporate edge is where the paths into terminal and airfield systems begin.

items.title: Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager has an exploited authentication bypass that gives an unauthenticated attacker administrator access — the controller that configures the links to outlying sites
items.content_text: Cisco published advisory cisco-sa-sdwan-webauth-xr8beuuU on 30 September for CVE-2026-76504 in Catalyst SD-WAN Manager, which Cisco rates CVSS 9.8. Improper handling of URI encoding lets a crafted request get past an authentication rule meant to restrict access to a particular API endpoint, giving a remote, unauthenticated attacker administrator-level access. Cisco says its PSIRT became aware of active exploitation in September 2026, and there are no workarounds. Fixed releases are 20.9.10.1, 20.12.8.2, 20.15.6.1, 20.18.4.1, 26.1.2.1 and 26.2.1; anything older than 20.9 has to migrate to a fixed release. Cisco revised the advisory to version 1.1 on 2 October. CISA added the flaw to KEV on 30 September with a 3 October federal deadline, which has passed. BleepingComputer counts it as the fifth exploited Catalyst SD-WAN zero-day of 2026. Cisco names no actor or victim, and no aviation organisation is named. Our assessment of the aviation angle is the same as for Arista’s VeloCloud Orchestrator: the SD-WAN manager is where configuration and policy for every edge router are set, and those edges can connect remote NAVAID and surveillance sites, fuel farms, cargo and MRO facilities and regional airports to the core network. Administrator access to the manager is a view of every site and possibly a way to change how traffic reaches each one.

items.title: MikroTik RouterOS: three exploited flaws in KEV, and now a CVSS 9.8 pre-authentication web-management flaw from CISA that is not reported exploited
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-67279 in MikroTik RouterOS to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 25 September, with a federal deadline of 28 September. KEV describes it as improper enforcement of a behavioural workflow in SSH that “could allow an unauthenticated client to open a session channel and send an exec request,” and notes that it can be chained to exploit CVE-2026-86060 without authentication. Coverage rates it CVSS 6.9, with no scoring version stated. It joins two RouterOS flaws CISA added on 10 September: CVE-2026-86060, an argument-injection flaw, and CVE-2026-67277, a missing-authentication flaw in the bandwidth-test service. CERT Polska’s posts of 5 September reported in-the-wild exploitation, from about 2 September, of a two-flaw SSH chain it calls “MikroTrick”. CERT Polska’s 22 September technical analysis names the chain: CVE-2026-67279 combined with CVE-2026-86060, which gives an unauthenticated attacker full administrative control. CVE-2026-67276, which earlier coverage tied to the chain, is not in KEV. Fixed builds are RouterOS 7.24.2, 7.23.4 and 6.49.21; the related CVE-2026-67278 needs 7.24.3 or 7.23.6, because the earlier fix was incomplete. Shadowserver counted more than 122,500 MikroTik devices with SSH reachable from the internet in early September; that is an exposure count, not a count of unpatched or compromised devices. No victims, sectors or actor have been named. The aviation relevance is breadth rather than any confirmed airport targeting: RouterOS boxes turn up in the inexpensive, quietly installed corners of an airport estate — remote stands and cargo sheds, car parks and shuttle depots, contractor site offices, CCTV and Wi-Fi backhaul — the places least likely to appear in an asset register and most likely to have an SSH port open for vendor support. Update, 29 September: CISA published ICS advisory ICSA-26-272-06 for a separate RouterOS flaw, CVE-2026-84411, a pre-authentication integer underflow in the web management interface that can lead to code execution or denial of service, rated CVSS v3.1 9.8 and v4 9.3. RouterOS before 7.24 is affected, and CISA lists 7.24 or later as fixed. It is not in KEV, no exploitation has been reported, and it is not part of the chain CERT Polska named.

items.title: A suspected Chinese espionage group exploited a BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day from late August; the fix shipped on 8 October
items.content_text: On 15 October Google’s threat intelligence group attributed zero-day exploitation of CVE-2026-102764 in BeyondTrust Remote Support to ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor formerly tracked as UNC5221, on the basis of overlapping tools and techniques. Exploitation began in late August. The flaw, rated CVSS v4 9.3 by BeyondTrust, lets attackers abuse the product’s internal messaging components to carry out file operations on Remote Support appliances; versions up to and including 26.2.3 are affected. BeyondTrust identified the defect in late September, shipped patch BT26-05-RS on 8 October and had patched its cloud-hosted customers by 9 October; self-hosted appliances without automatic updates must be patched by hand, and releases older than 24.3.1 must be upgraded first. SecurityWeek reports that two appliances were compromised, one hosted by BeyondTrust and one self-hosted. The attackers gained root, installed the SAWFLY PHP web shell and the BARECLAW SOCKS5 tunneller, harvested credentials, deleted logs and used the tool’s own file transfer to take documents from user desktops. Google names no victims for this activity, and the CVE was not in KEV as of the 15 October catalog. Our assessment: remote-support tools of this kind are how many IT providers and integrators reach airport and airline workstations, including machines that sit beside operational systems.

items.title: Palo Alto Networks fixes a PAN-OS zero-day that lets an authenticated attacker on the management interface run code as root — in KEV since 14 October
items.content_text: Palo Alto Networks disclosed CVE-2026-0322 on 14 October: a code-injection flaw that lets an authenticated attacker with network access to the PAN-OS management interface execute code as root on PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and on Panorama, with no special configuration required. The company found it internally, reports very limited exploitation aimed at the management interface and has published three US-based IP addresses tied to the attempts; it names no actor or timeline. Prisma Access and Cloud NGFW are not affected. Palo Alto scores it CVSS v4 8.6 for network access. Fixed releases include 12.2.4, 12.1.10-h2, 11.2.16, 11.1.16-h3 and 10.2.18-h12, with hotfixes for other branches. CISA added it to KEV the same day with a 17 October deadline. Separately, ReliaQuest warned on 9 October that Qilin and Settra ransomware operators are exploiting CVE-2026-0257, the older GlobalProtect authentication bypass Palo Alto disclosed in May, and that fixing it may not undo access gained before the patch. No aviation victim is named for either flaw. Our assessment: PAN-OS firewalls often sit on the boundary between airport or airline corporate networks and terminal and airfield systems, so root on the firewall means control of that boundary’s rules.

items.title: Attackers began probing SonicWall’s CVSS 10 SMA1000 flaw within two days of the fix; no successful breach has been confirmed
items.content_text: SonicWall published advisory SNWLID-2026-0017 with hotfixes on 6 October for CVE-2026-102255, a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the SMA1000 WorkPlace interface that lets an unauthenticated attacker make the appliance send requests to its own internal functions. CISA’s enrichment scores it CVSS v3.1 10.0 and SonicWall calls it maximum severity. Three authenticated flaws were fixed alongside it: an OS command injection, a Zip Slip in the management console and a stored cross-site scripting bug. Affected are SMA 6210, 7210 and 8200v appliances on 12.4.3-03526 or older and 12.5.0-02952 or older; fixed builds are 12.4.3-03670 and 12.5.0-03082. SMA 100 and firewall SSL VPN are not affected, and there is no workaround. Defused recorded the first hits on its decoy appliances on 8 October and Previdian logged 135 attempts from two US addresses. Reporting so far describes attempts, not confirmed compromises, and the flaw was not in KEV as of the 15 October catalog. SMA1000 appliances have been exploited repeatedly during 2026. Our assessment: SMA1000 is often the box through which vendors and integrators reach customer networks, which on an airport estate can include baggage, BMS and access-control systems.

items.title: October OT Patch Tuesday: unfixed critical web-server flaws across Siemens S7-1500 CPUs, and a Rockwell ArmorBlock I/O takeover bug
items.content_text: Siemens ProductCERT’s 13 October release, 17 advisories by SecurityWeek’s count, includes SSA-591731: eight web-server vulnerabilities in SIMATIC S7-1500, ET 200SP, ET 200pro and drive-controller CPUs, rated CVSS v3.1 9.6 and v4 9.4 by Siemens, that could let an attacker run code in an authorised user’s browser and carry out PLC operations with that user’s rights. All versions are affected and only mitigations exist so far. SSA-832641 fixes an authenticated path traversal in Industrial Edge devices (up to CVSS v3.1 9.1) for most models, but not yet for SCALANCE LPE9413/9433 or some HMI panels, and SSA-784472 lists 377 CVEs in the optional Linux subsystem of the S7-1500 TM MFP module, also without a fix. Rockwell’s SD1801 covers 1732E ArmorBlock I/O modules at 3.012 and earlier: CVE-2026-12655 (CVSS v3.1 9.1) lets an unauthenticated attacker change the module’s web-server password and take it over, and CVE-2026-12656 is a network-storm denial of service that needs a power cycle to clear; 3.013 fixes both. None of these is in KEV or reported exploited. Our assessment: PLC families and distributed I/O like these are common in conveyor and materials-handling automation, so check whether the integrators behind your baggage and building systems use them rather than assuming either way.

items.title: Two CISA advisories that list Transportation Systems have no fix: hard-coded credentials in EseeCloud cameras and end-of-life EasyIO FG building controllers
items.content_text: CISA’s 15 October advisory ICSA-26-288-02 covers Guangzhou Juan IoT’s EseeCloud app (4.9.6 and earlier) and firmware (4.9.86.0 and earlier), used in low-cost IP cameras and video recorders: hard-coded credentials rated CVSS v3.1 9.8, plus two medium-severity flaws. The vendor did not respond to CISA and no fix exists. CISA lists Transportation Systems among the sectors using it, alongside energy, communications, financial services and government. On 6 October CISA republished Johnson Controls’ JCI-PSA-2026-12 as ICSA-26-279-01, covering EasyIO FG controller firmware: hard-coded credentials and improper privilege management, each CVSS v3.1 7.7. The product is end of life, no fix will be issued and Johnson Controls advises moving to EasyIO Neo R1; CISA notes high attack complexity and that the flaws are not remotely exploitable, and it again lists Transportation Systems. This is a different product from the EasyIO Neo controllers fixed in CISA’s 1 October batch. Neither advisory reports exploitation, and none of the CVEs is in KEV. Our assessment: cheap cameras and recorders reach airport estates through car-park, concession and contractor installations, and building controllers through facilities projects, so both are ownership problems before they are patching problems.

items.title: A CVSS 10 command-injection flaw in VIVOTEK camera firmware covers 37 models and already has public proof-of-concept code — CISA lists Transportation Systems among the sectors that use them
items.content_text: CISA published ICSA-26-272-03 on 29 September for CVE-2026-22755, a command-injection flaw in VIVOTEK IP camera firmware affecting 37 camera models. It is rated CVSS v3.1 10.0 and v4 9.3, and public proof-of-concept code exists. The remedy is the latest firmware for each model. CISA lists Government Services and Facilities, Transportation Systems, Commercial Facilities, Energy, Critical Manufacturing and Financial Services among the sectors concerned, and reports no known exploitation. Nothing in the advisory names an airport. Our assessment of why it belongs here: IP cameras are among the most numerous networked devices on an airport estate, in terminals, car parks, cargo areas, aprons and along the perimeter, and they are usually installed and maintained by a security integrator rather than by IT. Public exploit code for a maximum-severity flaw shortens the time before someone scans for them, and a compromised camera is a foothold on the video network, which often shares cabling and switches with access control. The same 29 September batch of seven advisories also covered the Lantronix G520 cellular gateway, a new MikroTik RouterOS flaw, Toptech TMS7 and TopHAT terminal software, and three products for which no fix is planned: a Baicells LTE base station, an Anjvision product and the Viidure dashcam app.

items.title: CISA’s 1 October batch reaches terminal building systems: Armatura One access control ships an ActiveMQ flaw already exploited elsewhere, and Johnson Controls EasyIO building controllers get two fixes
items.content_text: CISA released six ICS advisories on 1 October, ICSA-26-274-01 to -06, and two cover building systems of the kind found in terminals. Armatura One, a physical access-control platform (-01), embeds a version of Apache ActiveMQ vulnerable to CVE-2023-46604, rated CVSS v3.1 9.8 and v4 10.0. That flaw is already in CISA’s KEV catalog because it was exploited against other ActiveMQ deployments, including by ransomware actors; CISA reports no exploitation of Armatura One itself. The same advisory lists a hard-coded cryptographic key (CVE-2026-94591) and hard-coded credentials (CVE-2026-94592), both 8.4 under v3.1 and 8.6 under v4, a log-exposure flaw (CVE-2026-94593, 7.8 and 8.5) and a lower-rated issue (CVE-2026-94594, 4.0). Versions before 4.7.2, and USA builds before 4.6.1, are affected; the fixes are 4.7.2 and 4.6.1_USA. CISA lists Transportation Systems among the sectors. Johnson Controls EasyIO Neo EC and CW building controllers (-04 and -05) have an information-exposure flaw, CVE-2026-64892 (3.5 under v3.1, 6.3 under v4), and cleartext transmission of sensitive data, CVE-2026-64893 (5.4 and 7.3), fixed in EC V3.3b64 and CW V3.3b26; CISA again lists Transportation Systems. The rest of the batch: Monta’s EV-charging platform (-02), whose missing authentication on a WebSocket channel, CVE-2026-95102 (9.4 under v3.1, 9.3 under v4), allows charging-station impersonation and has no fixed version, only configuration guidance — Monta points to OCPP 1.6 Security Profile 2 and says rate limiting is in place; ABB PCM600 up to 2.14 (-03), with a privilege-escalation and a path-traversal flaw, a workaround and no fixed version; and the Meari IoT cloud platform (-06), with no fix planned. CISA reports no known exploitation for any of the six. No airport is named. Our assessment: access control and building management are airport OT in everything but name, usually run by facilities and security contractors, and an access-control server with hard-coded keys and credentials is a direct route to doors, turnstiles and badge records. EV chargers appear in airport car parks and electric ground-support fleets, which is why the Monta item is listed here.

items.title: A signature-check flaw in Lantronix G520 cellular gateways could let an attacker replace the software and run code as root — the kind of box that connects an airport’s outlying sites
items.content_text: CISA published ICSA-26-272-01 on 29 September for two flaws in Lantronix G520 Series cellular gateways running 2.6.0.4R6_stable: CVE-2026-91191, improper verification of a cryptographic signature, and CVE-2026-84409, a cross-site scripting flaw, each rated CVSS v3.1 7.5 and v4 7.7. CISA says exploitation could allow an attacker to replace software and execute arbitrary code with root privileges. The fix is release 2.6.0.7R6. CISA lists Transportation Systems, Energy, and Water and Wastewater as the sectors concerned and reports no known exploitation. No airport or airline is named. Our assessment of the aviation angle: cellular gateways are how sites without fixed lines get connected, and on an airport estate that tends to mean the edges — car-park pay stations and barriers, remote stands, fuel-farm and pump-station telemetry, construction compounds and contractor remote-support links — often installed by whoever built the site and missing from the network inventory. A gateway that accepts replaced software is a persistent foothold at exactly the places least watched.

items.title: Arista’s VeloCloud SD-WAN orchestrator has a CVSS 10 flaw under active attack — the console that configures the links to your outlying sites
items.content_text: Arista published Security Advisory 0183 on 22 September for CVE-2026-93952, an improper input validation flaw in on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO), rated CVSS 10.0 under v3.1 and 9.5 under v4.0. Arista says the flaw “may allow a remote attacker to access privileged internal functionality and impact the VCO host” and that it is “known to be actively exploited.” Exposure depends on configuration. An attacker needs certificate-based authentication to be set up between VeloCloud Edges and the orchestrator, the public part of an Edge’s authentication certificate, and network access to the VCO web interface; “VCO tenant or operator credentials are not required.” Vulnerable on-prem releases are 5.2.3.15 and earlier, 6.1.3.7 and earlier, 6.4.2.7 and earlier, and 7.0.0.2 and earlier. Fixes are in 5.2.3.16 and 6.4.2.8, and at publication Arista listed no fixed build for the 6.1 or 7.0 trains; check the advisory for later releases. Hosted and dedicated VCO instances have already been patched. Arista publishes indicators: the files /usr/local/sbin/.vcnode.js and /usr/local/sbin/vc-sysmond (MD5 dc78e206eaeadec59fc5801fe4556bd0), a vc-sysmon systemd service, an x-vc-opt HTTP header, and the source addresses 142.93.149.77 and 104.248.126.159. CISA added the flaw to KEV on 22 September with a 25 September deadline. No aviation victim is named. The aviation angle is architectural. An SD-WAN orchestrator pushes configuration and policy to every edge it manages, and those edges can connect remote NAVAID and surveillance sites, fuel farms, cargo and MRO facilities, and regional airports to the core network. Compromising the orchestrator gives an attacker a view of every site and possibly a way into each one.

items.title: An F5 BIG-IP APM overflow gives unauthenticated code execution, but only where APM acts as an OAuth authorisation server — and it is being exploited
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-94127 in F5 BIG-IP Access Policy Manager to the KEV catalog on 22 September, with a federal deadline of 25 September. The flaw is a heap-based buffer overflow rated CVSS 9.8 under v3.1 and 9.3 under v4.0 that allows unauthenticated remote code execution. It is covered by F5 advisory K000162605. Exposure is narrower than the score suggests. Rapid7’s analysis says a system is exposed only when a virtual server has both an APM access policy and an OAuth profile attached, so that APM is acting as an OAuth authorisation server. F5 has issued engineering hotfixes for the 21.1.0, 17.5.0 and 17.1.0 branches. Rapid7 reported no confirmed public proof-of-concept as of 22 September, and F5 has published no attribution or victim count. No aviation victim is named. It belongs on this page because BIG-IP APM is widely used as the access gateway in front of web portals and vendor remote access, the role it can play for crew, engineering and MRO applications and for integrator access into airport systems, and in an OAuth-server role it issues the tokens those applications trust.

items.title: Cisco’s network access control server has a CVSS 10 authentication bypass under active attack — this is the box that decides which devices get onto which airport network
items.content_text: Cisco published advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 on 16 September for CVE-2026-76460, a CVSS 10.0 flaw in Identity Services Engine and ISE-PIC that lets an unauthenticated remote attacker bypass the web-based management interface through an API endpoint with insufficient authentication. Cisco states its PSIRT “is aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability.” All versions are affected; fixes are 3.1 Patch 12, 3.2 Patch 11, 3.3 Patch 12, 3.4 Patch 7 and 3.5 Patch 4. There are no workarounds — restricting management traffic with infrastructure access control lists is the only mitigation short of patching. CISA added the CVE to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 16 September with an unusually short three-day federal remediation deadline of 19 September, which has now passed. No attribution has been published and no critical-infrastructure or aviation targeting has been claimed; Singapore’s Cyber Security Agency issued its own alert on 21 September urging immediate patching. The reason it matters here is architectural rather than reported: where an airport or airline estate runs 802.1X and posture-based access control, ISE is the policy engine that decides which contractor laptop, handheld or engineering workstation lands on a terminal, baggage or airside VLAN — so administrative control of it is control of the segmentation itself.

items.title: A Zyxel small-office switch flaw enters KEV after 996 devices in 48 countries were harvested for configurations and credentials — the kit in the corners of an airport nobody inventories
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-7273 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 21 September with a federal remediation deadline of 24 September. The flaw is a stack-based buffer overflow in the CGI program of Zyxel’s GS1900-series managed switches — GS1900-8, 8HP, 10HP, 16, 24, 24E, 24EP, 24HPv2, 48 and 48HPv2 — that lets an unauthenticated attacker on the LAN execute operating-system commands with a crafted HTTP request; Zyxel patched it on 16 June in firmware 2.90(AAHH.2)C0 and per-model equivalents, and publishes no CVSS score for it. GreyNoise research published on 21 September documents what it describes as the first in-the-wild exploitation: a single actor assessed as Chinese-speaking compromised 996 GS1900 switches across 48 countries from about mid-August — Italy, the United States, Taiwan, France, South Korea and the Netherlands lead the count — using an obfuscated Python tool that pulled device configurations and root-level hashed credentials over TFTP; 564 of the victims were still on factory-default credentials. The same actor stole records from an unnamed western government organisation through two WordPress flaws and also targeted Gitea CVE-2026-60004, among other products; GreyNoise describes the switch actor as “the same or related to” the group Acronis calls Red Heron, based on shared infrastructure, malware and tactics; treat that as GreyNoise’s assessment rather than a confirmed attribution. KEV lists the flaw as LAN-based, so the practical exposure is any path that reaches the switch’s management interface. That is the aviation angle: GS1900-class switches are what a contractor site office, a car-park attendant booth, a retail concession or a CCTV closet gets fitted with, they rarely appear in an asset register, and a stolen configuration is a map of every VLAN the switch carries plus the credentials to reach it.

items.title: Twenty flaws in Pepperl+Fuchs IO-Link masters, two at CVSS 9.8 — and the same firmware ships under Phoenix Contact and Carlo Gavazzi badges
items.content_text: CERT@VDE published VDE-2026-014 on 16 September: Pepperl+Fuchs has fixed 20 vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-27546 to CVE-2026-27565, in the firmware of its ICE2-8IOL and ICE3-8IOL IO-Link master modules, found by Nozomi Networks Labs researchers, with the fix in firmware 1.7.8. The two worst are CVE-2026-27546, an authentication bypass, and CVE-2026-27565, unauthenticated upload of a malicious IODD device-description file that executes shell scripts, both at CVSS 9.8. Most of the rest, CVE-2026-27547 through -27564, are command-injection, file-inclusion and authorisation flaws between 7.2 and 8.8 that lead to root-level code execution on the module; CVE-2026-27557 at 7.5 is an unauthenticated path traversal that reads the module’s SSH server private keys, and CVE-2026-27553 at 6.5 discloses password hashes. The same firmware is sold rebadged, so the exposure is wider than one vendor: Phoenix Contact IOL MA8 PN DI8 and IOL MA8 EIP DI8 masters carry the same 20 CVEs under VDE-2026-027, and Carlo Gavazzi YL212 and YN115 masters are covered by VDE-2026-028, all with the same 1.7.8 fix and the same date. Nozomi Networks Labs published its own technical write-up on 24 September, covering 19 of the CVEs on the ICE2-8IOL-K45P-RJ45 and describing how, chained, they give an unauthenticated attacker root on the module and the ability to manipulate sensor and actuator data. No exploitation is reported, and the flaws did not appear in CISA’s ICS advisory batches through 24 September. Our assessment of the aviation relevance, since no airport is named: IO-Link is the sensor and actuator layer of modern conveyor and sortation systems, and baggage-handling systems are assembled by integrators from exactly this class of discrete-automation component. A master module that gives root to anyone who can reach its web interface is a foothold on the PROFINET or EtherNet/IP segment that runs the belts.

items.title: CISA’s 22 September batch brings nine advisories, and two of them are airport-terminal systems: Siemens Desigo CC building management and Siveillance Control security management
items.content_text: CISA released nine ICS advisories on Tuesday 22 September, ICSA-26-265-01 through -09. Two cover the lwIP embedded TCP/IP stack: an out-of-bounds write in its MQTT client application, reported by Shahriyar Jalayeri of ByteRay (-01), and a double free, reported by Eric Evenchick of Tetrel Security (-02). Six are Siemens: Siveillance Control, an unrestricted upload of a file with a dangerous type (-03); SIPLUS and SIMATIC products affected by the third-party Linux “Copy Fail” flaw (-04); the Desigo CC family, a code injection reported by Michelin CERT (-05); Industrial Edge Management, a third-party weak password-recovery issue (-06); SIMOVE Fleetmanager and SIPLANT, a relative path traversal (-07); and WTV676 and WTV776, improper validation of a specified type of input (-08). The last is OpenPLC, a cross-site scripting flaw (-09). For this page, two of those matter most. Desigo CC is Siemens’ building-management platform and sits over HVAC, fire and energy systems in many terminals. Siveillance Control is a security-management platform that brings access control, video and alarms together in a control room. We could not reach CISA’s own advisory pages at generation time. CVE numbers, CVSS scores, fix availability and CISA’s sector listings are therefore deliberately left out rather than taken from secondary digests; read each advisory before prioritising. No exploitation has been reported for anything in the batch. Update for this edition: the lwIP MQTT advisory (-01) is now verified from CISA’s advisory data as CVE-2026-87121, rated CVSS v3.1 9.8 and v4 9.3, in lwIP MQTT 2.0.1 to 2.2.1; it was not in KEV as of 1 October. The other eight advisories remain as described above.

items.title: Nozomi finishes its Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 research: twelve flaws, several chainable to root on an OT edge device — patched, unexploited, and older than it looks
items.content_text: Correction to the previous edition. This entry previously read as a new critical disclosure dated 15 September. It was not. The underlying CVEs were disclosed in May 2025 under CISA advisory ICSA-25-135-18; what happened on 15 September was a CISA update to that advisory, adding the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client and vendor fixes. The research behind it published in two parts: the first, on 10 September, covered four PROFINET Discovery and basic Configuration Protocol memory-corruption flaws in the SCALANCE LPE9403 — an uninitialised value, a NULL pointer dereference and two out-of-bounds reads, each rated CVSS 5.3 and each a denial of service rather than code execution. The second part, published by Nozomi Networks Labs on 18 September, gives the full picture: twelve vulnerabilities in total, nine in the device firmware rated between 5.3 and 8.5 and three in the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client rated between 6.7 and 8.5. Nozomi demonstrated that several of them can be chained to obtain root-level control of the device, which in an OT context means manipulating telemetry, suppressing alarms, reading operational data, disrupting services and moving laterally. Affected are LPE9403 firmware below V4.0 HF0 and the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client through V2.1; Siemens has published advisories and fixes, with V4.0 HF0 and later the fixed firmware. There is no evidence of exploitation in the wild. For aviation the relevance is where these devices sit: the LPE9403 is a local-processing engine used as a PROFINET edge collector, and where an integrator has put one into baggage, plant-room, BMS or airfield equipment, root on it is root inside the segment that equipment lives in.

items.title: Rockwell extends its lock-out recovery guidance to Micro820 and Micro850 — the small PLCs in the parts of an airport that never get a security review
items.content_text: Rockwell Automation revised security notice SD1790 for a fifth time on 18 September. The notice, first published on 30 July, is titled as hardening guidance and instructions for restoring access when a controller’s password is unknown, and revision 5.0 extends the recovery and hardening instructions to Micro820 and Micro850 controllers alongside the MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 it already covered. It exists because of the FBI’s public service announcement of 30 July, which described attackers remotely altering the configuration of internet-exposed PLCs, changing IP addresses and setting passwords where none had existed, locking operators out of their own controllers. There is no CVE; the guidance is to remove controllers from direct internet exposure, reach them through a VPN and firewall isolation, set strong passwords, keep offline project backups, disable the controller’s HTTP server and keep firmware current. Revision 5.0 adds no new incident data and names no sector; Rockwell has published no new vulnerability advisories since its 1 September batch. Our assessment of why it belongs here: MicroLogix and Micro800 controllers are the PLCs of small standalone plant — car-park barriers and pay-on-foot systems, pump stations, fuel-farm ancillaries, de-icing fluid recovery, packaged HVAC — typically installed by a mechanical or electrical contractor with a cellular router for remote support, and typically absent from the airport’s own asset register. The FBI’s scenario, a controller that suddenly has a password its owner does not know, is the one those sites are least prepared to recover from.

items.title: GAO finds only 7 of 22 civilian agencies fully meet federal rules for managing networked IoT and OT devices — and an industry coalition now asks CISA for a binding OT directive
items.content_text: GAO-26-108937, published on 30 September, reviewed how 22 civilian CFO Act agencies manage networked Internet of Things and OT devices against OMB requirements that date from December 2023, were updated in January 2025 and carried a September 2024 completion deadline. Fifteen agencies had established device inventories, 11 maintained them, 10 included all the required information, and only seven fully met all three requirements. No agency reported an IoT cybersecurity waiver. GAO notes that OMB has not issued updated guidance covering fiscal year 2026 and makes one recommendation: that OMB issue updated guidance covering networked IoT and OT devices and oversee its implementation. On 6 October CyberScoop reported that the OT Cybersecurity Coalition is urging CISA to issue a binding operational directive focused solely on OT security at federal agencies, citing the GAO findings and this summer’s water-utility attacks. The coalition wants an accountable OT cybersecurity officer at each agency, minimum practices drawn from existing federal guidance, alignment with CISA’s 2022 Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals, and a review of whether NSA’s OT guidance should apply to civilian agencies. This is a proposal only. CISA has announced no directive and did not respond to CyberScoop. For aviation readers the relevance is indirect. GAO’s numbers show how hard it is to keep even an inventory of networked devices current, which is the same first step airport OT programmes struggle with, and a federal OT directive, if one were issued, would become a public reference point for what a minimum OT programme looks like.

items.title: GAO’s industry panel says overlapping federal cyber-reporting rules can pull responders away from the incident — and the CIRCIA final rule has reached White House review
items.content_text: The Government Accountability Office published GAO-26-109197, “Cybersecurity Regulations: Industry Panelists Identify Duplication and Conflicts and Ways to Address Them”, on 28 September. It reports a virtual panel held on 16 July with six industry representatives from energy, financial services, and healthcare and public health. Panelists said it could be hard to meet every reporting requirement while also remediating a cyber threat, saw DHS and SEC rules as duplicating sector rules, and half of them agreed that progress on harmonisation had been limited. Their suggestions were consistent timeframes, thresholds and definitions; a lead agency such as CISA to coordinate reporting; and closer government–industry collaboration. The report makes no formal recommendations, and transportation was not on the panel. Separately, CISA has sent its final rule under the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act (CIRCIA) to the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, which logged it for review on 1 October; the text is not public and the rule is not yet in the Federal Register. The statutory deadline was October 2025 and CISA’s later targets of May and September 2026 slipped; HIPAA Journal reports publication is expected before the end of the year, and the text can still change in review. Once in force it would require covered incidents to be reported within 72 hours and ransom payments within 24 hours; any text quoted today as the rule is the 2024 proposal. For aviation the relevance is practical: airports, airlines and their service providers can answer to several regulators for the same incident, and the harmonisation question the panel raised is the one an incident team meets in its first hours.

items.title: CISA’s Cybersecurity Awareness Month campaign, “Securing the Next 250”, asks operators to reduce, replace and recover — and replacing end-of-support kit is the hard part for airport OT
items.content_text: CISA launched “Securing the Next 250” at the start of Cybersecurity Awareness Month, as reported by Industrial Cyber on 2 October. The campaign frames its advice for organisations as three Rs: reduce attack surfaces, replace end-of-support devices, and recover quickly to keep operations running. For individuals it repeats four practices: avoid and report phishing, use strong passwords, use multifactor authentication with a password manager, and keep software updated. Acting Director Nick Andersen tied the campaign to the knock-on effect of disruption: when critical infrastructure fails, the businesses and communities that depend on it fail with it. It is a voluntary awareness campaign, not a rule or directive, and it sets no sector-specific requirement. For airports the useful part is the middle R. Terminal OT often includes devices past their support life — ageing BMS front ends, baggage-control workstations, access-control servers and controllers fitted at construction — and replacing them runs on capital-project timescales, not patch cycles.

items.title: CISA and FBI on integrator risk: one compromised automation vendor, about 800 files of its customers’ SCADA details — and transportation among those customers
items.content_text: CISA and the FBI publicised a joint fact sheet on 24 September, Considerations for Critical Infrastructure Operators Working With Third-Party ICS Integrators; the document itself is dated 23 September. It cites a case in which foreign cyber actors, between March and April 2025, compromised a US industrial automation company that provided system integration, engineering consulting and SCADA programming services to customers including power utilities and transportation entities. On the integrator’s network the actors searched for terms including “customers” and “SCADA” and packaged approximately 800 files — customer SCADA information, ICS device details and schematics — into nine archive files. The fact sheet names neither the integrator, its customers nor the actor, and describes no disruption. Its recommendations are least privilege for every integrator connection, on-demand remote access that the operator authorises and can monitor, and contract terms covering data storage, remote access and patching. No airport, airline or air navigation service provider is named, and this is guidance, not a new incident. It is carried here because airport ground OT is among the most integrator-dependent estates in transport: baggage handling, jet bridges, airfield lighting, fuel systems and terminal BMS are typically installed and supported by a specialist integrator who holds the drawings, the configurations and a standing way in — the same asset class the 2025 case shows is worth stealing even when the operator’s own network is never touched.

items.title: NIST opens its OT security guide for revision: the SP 800-82 Rev. 4 draft expands to building automation and industrial IoT, with comments due 30 November
items.content_text: NIST released the initial public draft of SP 800-82 Revision 4, “Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security”, on 21 September, with comments open until 30 November 2026. The draft is reorganised around the Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, with the risk section refocused on the Govern function, and it expands the guidance on asset management, network monitoring and zero-trust architecture. Its coverage grows to building automation and control systems, water and wastewater, food and agriculture, freight rail, maritime vessels, and the convergence of industrial IoT with cloud services. Aviation is not among the sectors named. The building-automation material is the part that maps most directly onto an airport, because terminal HVAC, lighting, fire and access-control integration are building-automation systems, and they are often the least governed OT on the estate. This is draft guidance, not a requirement, and it places no new obligation on airports or airlines.

items.title: CISA publishes a cyber-decoys guide — the rare detection control you can add to an airport network without touching what it controls
items.content_text: CISA released “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” on 17 September. The guide defines decoys as assets that look like legitimate systems, accounts or data but exist to distract an adversary, reveal their presence, or collect intelligence on how they operate, and it sets out three phases: preparation, execution and analysis. CISA positions the technique alongside Zero Trust rather than as a replacement for it. The reason it reads well for aviation is the constraint every airport security team knows: you cannot install an agent on a baggage controller, a jet-bridge PLC or an airfield-lighting panel, and a change window on those systems is expensive. A decoy is additive — a fake engineering workstation, a planted credential that no legitimate process should ever use, a file share named to look like integrator documentation — and it produces a signal with almost no false positives, because nothing legitimate should touch it. The catch is that a decoy nobody monitors is decoration, so the alerting path matters more than the decoy.
